analysis.one_liner: Restores the DEA's power to immediately freeze suspicious opioid shipments.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-page bill would repeal the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2016 and restore the Controlled Substances Act language that law replaced. The 2016 law raised the bar the DEA had to meet before it could immediately suspend a drug distributor's registrations and freeze suspicious opioid shipments. Repealing it would give DEA back its earlier, faster enforcement tools against companies shipping unusually large quantities of prescription opioids.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic, and DEA enforcement staff, who would regain the authority to move quickly against distributors shipping suspicious volumes of opioid pills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Public Law 114-145 in full and restores the Controlled Substances Act provisions that law had amended, as if it had never been enacted [S3].
Under the restored provisions, DEA regains the stronger, pre-2016 standard for taking immediate action against registrants whose orders show the kind of volume patterns tied to diversion [S2].

The bill was introduced in the same month as major news reporting that the 2016 law had hampered DEA's ability to freeze suspicious opioid shipments (the 60 Minutes/Washington Post investigation published in October 2017).

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale drug distributors and opioid manufacturers, who would face faster DEA suspensions and heightened scrutiny of large shipments; some pharmacies and hospice suppliers argued the 2016 law protected legitimate patients from supply disruptions.

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the 2016 law, including pharmacy and hospice groups, argued it prevented DEA from cutting off legitimate pain patients' medication supplies on thin evidence, and this bill would reverse those protections [S2].

Some analysts argued the 2016 law's changes were modest and that pinning the opioid epidemic on it overstated its effect; a one-line full repeal offered no replacement standard, only the pre-2016 status quo [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If passed, the bill would hand DEA back a fast enforcement tool at real cost to distributors in suspended shipments, but the trade-off is blunt: a full repeal restores the old standard wholesale rather than fixing the standard, so legitimate suppliers would face the same speed. Weighing lives against distributor convenience, most public-health advocates would call that trade worth making; the unresolved question is whether the 2016 law did as much damage as its critics claimed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to their subcommittees, was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the bill on October 23, 2017 [S1].

It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, and within days to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations [S5].
No further action was recorded, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill ever reaching a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale drug distributors and opioid manufacturers are better off: the weaker 2016 enforcement standard stayed in place, and DEA never regained the immediate-suspension tool through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the 2016 drug enforcement law and restore the prior Controlled Substances Act standard.

against.name: Wholesale drug distributors
against.role: McKesson, Cardinal Health, AmerisourceBergen and the industry coalition behind the 2016 law
against.what_they_did: Spent years lobbying for the 2016 law that weakened DEA's ability to freeze suspicious opioid shipments; the October 2017 60 Minutes/Washington Post investigation of that campaign appeared the same week this repeal bill was introduced, and the repeal drew no cosponsors and died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred and no other member signed on: a single Democrat sponsored the bill and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no party-level position was ever recorded.

industries.note: Repealing the 2016 law would end the higher evidence bar these companies won in 2016, exposing them again to immediate DEA suspension of shipments flagged as suspicious. Their core interest in keeping the weaker standard runs against the public's interest in faster enforcement against pill dumping.

Tighter scrutiny of distributor orders narrows the pipeline for the mass pill shipments that fed the epidemic, cutting into sales volume. Their interest in continued loose oversight is at odds with the public's.

The 2016 law's backers argued it protected legitimate pharmacies and hospice patients from abrupt DEA cutoffs; this repeal would restore the pre-2016 standard under which some lawful suppliers were penalized. Their access concern is real, but it was also the stated rationale for weakening enforcement.
